QUINCY, Ill., May 14.—"Windy Dicky" and four of his gang of thieves and pick-pockets were run in this morning by the police. THREATENED LYNCHING.

Sheriff Vanpeel has been forwarned of meetings being held with that object, and has garrisoned the jail with a force of officers well armed, and declares that he intends to fight if necessary. MURDER AND SUICIDE.
ATCHISON, Ks., May 16.—While Lou Gwinne, a waitress at Walker's restaurant, was standing in the yard in the rear of the restaurant, her husband, Charley Gwinne, a cook at the Atlantic hotel, approached and after a few words drew a revolver and fired three shots at her, two of the balls entering her breast and the third piercing her brain and causing instant death. MEDETATED LYNCHING.
GRAND HAVEN, Mich., May 16.—There is great excitement here caused by a report that an organized body of about two hundred men are on the way to take Albertus Voskamp, who murdered Hiram H. Coady near Coopersville, out of jail and hang him. Sheriff Vanpeel has been forewarned of meetings being held with that object, and has garrisoned the jail with a force of officers well armed.

LATER.—4 p. m.—The three hundred men made their appearance about midnight, and were greatly surprised to find a company of the state militia drawn up in front of the jail. District Attorney McBride made them a speech and invited a few of them inside to inspect the make up of the jail and arrangements for defending the building, after which they concluded they could not get the prisoner without blood being shed, and they returned home at 2 a. m. BLOODY BALTIMORE.

BALTIMORE, May 16.—To-day has been marked by more bloodshed than has ever occurred in Baltimore for years. About 4:15 yesterday afternoon Edward Lucas, a bricklayer, stabbed Dennis Bradner, an oyster dredger, in the side, inflicting a wound from which he died in ten minutes. Lucas was arrested.

About 6:30 Police Officer Campbell shot at an escaped prisoner named EdCarr, near Green Mount cemetery and the ball struck him in the back and made a dangerous wound.

About 9 o'clock Saturday evening, Paul Rossi, (Italian) seriously stabbed Henry Toping in the left side, near the heart. There was no provocation for the deed. Rossi was arrested. About 8:50 p. m., Officer Wardell was attacked by a crowd of roughs, who took his club away and knocked him down. He fired a shot in the air and a private watchman, James Jameson, came to his assistance, and fired three shots into the crowd. One of the balls struck Henry Cleveland in the left thigh, inflicting a serious wound, and another ball struck Stephen Hasty in his right arm. Both were only innocent lookers-on.

MURDER OF A WOMAN.

HOBOKEN, N. J., May 16.—Lost night the body of a woman was found in a clump of woods, between the Bergen and Guttenburg roads. The body was, to all appearances, that of an attractive young woman, with a German cast of face and an attractive figure. The back of her head was smashed in and her dark hair was clotted with blood. Her clothing was covered with mud and grass, and showed that her struggle for life had been of a most desperate character. A gash three inch long had been cut over the right eye and the clothing was bodily torn, but it could be seen that it was of superior quality. An air of refinement about the features, even in the distortion of death agony, showed that she was superior to the class of people who inhabited the vicinity. Near the body were two large stones, weighing thirty pounds each. On one of which was clotted blood and dark hair, which showed that they were the implements used by the fiends who did the work. The body was taken to the morgue.

Christina Cuttle, only daughter o James Cuttle, a well-to-do farmer o Guttenberg, has been missing for some time, and is supposed to be the deceased. She has been intimate with Judson Francoir, ex-constable of that town, who was recently held for trial before Justice Plumstead. She has been absent from her home off and on for a month, and, it is reported, gave birth to a child in New York City. Neither the girl nor the ex-constable could be found. The father of the girl believes that the deceased is his dargler, but is not sure of it.

LYNCH LAW.
state news column.
In our State news column mention is made of the whipping and shooting to death, by a mob, of a man incarcerated in jail at Jeannerette, St. Mary parish, on a charge of chicken stealing. The jail was forced open and the prisoner taken out and flogged. According to one report the petty malefactor was then hanged, but another and more probable version is that he broke away from his persecutors and was shot down while attempting to escape. This is properly characterized by the Iberia papers as a brutal murder, having no shadow of justification, and for the good name of the parish in which the dastardly crime was committed, it is to be hoped the cowardly perpetrators will be ferreted out and punished. The disposition of irresponsible mobs to supercede the laws and constitute themselves judges, juries and executioners, is a crying evil and a disgrace to our country that every good citizen has an interest in suppressing.

Those who are disposed to approve of or wink at the methods of Judge Lynch in cases where the victims have committed great crimes and there is no doubt of guilt, should be warned by the Iberia occurrence that the precedent is a dangerous one under any circumstances and ought not to be tolerated. Our government is one of law and order; every violator of its laws is, in a greater or lesser degree, a public enemy; and the men that break into a prison to kill or maltreat defenceless captives—who are entitled to judicial trial and are presumed to be innocent until proven guilty—must be ranked with the worst classes of law breakers and deserve punishment accordingly.

Hung by a Mob.
A few days ago a colored man named Ben Robertson was arrested and confined to jail in the town of Jeannette on a charge of chicken stealing, and during the night was assaulted, taken out by a mob and hung. The offense was not deserving of so grave a punishment, and besides as he was in the hands of the law, it was a very felonious act, to say the least, on the part of those who did the hanging. The Colonel of our parish, Dr. T. J. Woolf, made an inquest on the body and gave a verdict in accordance with the facts stated above. We have no recollection of such brutal treatment to a prisoner in the hands of the law, and we cannot explain why a man should thus perish for stealing a few chickens, when so many others are liberated for darker crimes. TRIPLE MURDER.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

ATLANTA, Ga., Aug. 10.—Near Dawson, in Terrell County, yesterday was enacted a triple murder, the motive of which was robbery. The details appear to be that a negro named Frank Hudson called at the house of an old white man named David Lee, who it was known kept a good sum of money in his house. Fluding Lee at home, with a view of decoying him away from the house, he told him that his field fence, a short distance from his residence, was on fire. Lee started for the scene, accompanied by Hudson, who offered, to assist him in putting out the flames. The negro, before going, picked up an ax, stating he would probably need it to cut away the burning portion. Soon after leaving the house and while on the way to the place where the fence was said to be burning, Hudson struck Lee a terrible blow on the head with the ax, splitting his head open and killing him instantly. He then returned to the house, when he killed Mrs. Lee and servant with the same ax, and also struck down with the same weapon another servant girl, leaving her as he supposed in a dying condition. Hudson then robbed the house, getting $500 as the proceeds of his fledglish crime, and left. An hour later a neighbor called and found the fourth victim of Hudson in a recovering condition, and she detailed what had occurred, and soon the entire neighborhood was alarmed and out in search of Hudson, who, if captured, will be lynched.

PROBABLY LYNCHED.
ATLANTA, Ga., Aug. 20.—Your correspondent yesterday telegraphed the details then at hand relative to the brutal murder of David Lee and wife, two old and respectable citizens of Terrell County, and also the killing of a negro woman and the probably fatal wounding of another negro woman by Frank Hudson (colored), who committed the crime for the purpose of robbing the Lees' residence and leaving no living witnesses to tell the tale. Hudson, after committing the crime, fled and was pursued by Sherid Edwards, of Dougherty County, and Marshal Westbrook, two of the best detectives in that section of the State. He was overhauled on Bates' plantation, in Lee County, and taken to Albany, where he was landed in jail. The fact that the murder was of a most unprovoked character, and that he had killed both white and colored people, carried the indignation of both races wild, both together assuming a formidable shape. The indignation was so strong that considerable fears were entertained for the safety of Hudson by the authorities. The Guards were called out by Mayor Wilder, but refused to respond, giving as an excuse that the Mayor had no authority to call out the military. It is said that this would not have stopped them bad they any desire to protect the negro, but that public sentiment was so strongly in favor of lynch law that they did not care to interfere and prevent it being administered. The Governor was telegraphed by the Sherif, asking him to authorize the Albany Guards to turn out and guard the jail for the purpose of protecting the life of Hudson, but, as the Governor was out of the city, there was no one to act in his place, and it is believed here that ere this Hudson has been lynched. If this be so, no effort will be made to bring the lynchers before the courts, as public sentiment will crush such a thing out.

PITTSBURG, Aug. 20.—At the hearing in the Mollie Maguires murder case at Union-town to-day four witnesses were examined, the most important being William McDowell and Robert Long. McDowell testified to being present at the license hearing in Dunbar on June 11, when there were present also Healy, Kane, and Collins. The latter presented McFarland's license petition to McDowell with the request to sign it, which was refused. He then asked Healy to sign it, who also refused, telling him to go away with his whisky gang. Hot words ensued, and Healy withdrew. Collins again approached McDowell, who to get rid of him said: "Get Healy to sign it and then I will." and Collins replied, "God damn him, he'll be attended to." Kane then stepped up and added: "Yes, as soon as this license question is settled, you — — —, he'll be attended to." Robert King deposed that while returning from the dedication of a Catholic church in Scottdale about the 1st of June, he and Healy were approached by Kane in the cars. Kane said to Healy: "If you try to ruin me and my family I'll whip the head off of you, by God! I mean to do it." The testimony of Ella Casey and John Bunting was unimportant, except to establish the presence of Rogan, McFarland, Flood, the two Dolans, and two unrecognized men in the neighborhood of the murder. This closed the hearing. After a review of the testimony, respective counsel, the Court decided that Martin Donohoe be discharged, that John Kane be remanded, and that the rest be admitted to bail, as follows: James McFarland and Pat Dolan in the sum of $5,000 each, John Collins in $3,000, and Mike Dolan, Bernard Flood, and James Rogan in $500 each. It is not likely any of them will be able to obtain bail except McFarland. The friends of the prisoners are not very well pleased with this decision.

New steel rails have been laid on the Georgia Railroad from Augusta as far as Greensboro. This is certainly a great improvement, and renders travel on this road much more pleasant.

According to an account given by the Albany News, Frank Hudson, alias Arthur Wade, the negro murderer of the Lee family in Terrell county, had a stormy trip to and reception at Dawson after his arrest in Lee county. Every station along the road was crowded with excited people endeavoring to see the prisoner, but he was locked securely in one of the cars. At Brown's station twenty-five or thirty men from Terrell entered the cars, but did not see the prisoner. At Dawson he was taken out and literally borne away by one thousand five hundred or two thousand persons of both colors, equally bent on his immediate execution, to the court house, where he was thrown from the doorway to the ground and finally placed on a table to narrate the horrors of the butchery. He was so frightened and overcome by the furious demonstration that he fainted, which created a pausa. Prominent citizens took advantage of this, addressed the crowd in stirring appeals for law and order, which was finally restored, and the prisoner lodged in jail.

The Twiggs county tragedy, in which it was supposed that the orphan boy Charles Arnold committed suicide by hanging, seems about to develop new features, and turn out one of the most atrocious of murders. It is now stated that his home with Mr. Jones was very unhappy, and that on the same day he disappeared he was severely beaten by a son of Mr. Jones. Near where he was found tied to the limb of a tree, about thirty feet from the ground, was a rope, and under the rope were several of the dead boy's teeth. On some bushes near was his shirt, and it is stated that a bullet hole was found in the back. The shirt was stained with blood. His body having been moved from the tree, where he must have been murdered, shows conclusively that he was not the instrument of his own death. The citizens of Twiggs are said to be greatly incensed upon these discoveries, and it is gratifying to know that a searching investigation is in progress by the grand jury.

CINCINNATI, August 22. — A dispatch to the Commercial from Atlanta, Ga., says that on last Tuesday night, in Terrell county, Frank Hudson, a bad negro, went to the farm house of Daniel Lee after the family had retired and told Lee that his woods were on fire and fences burning. He went out with Lee, but soon returned with an axe, which he had brought upon his first call. He demanded supper of Mrs. Lee. She refused and he felled her with the axe, tilling her instantly. The only persons in the house were two colored girls. They heard the noise and rushed into the room where Mrs. Lee was lying dead. Hudson felled both with the axe and left them for dead. He then stole $00 and fled. The blows from the axe had killed one of the colored girls, but had only stunned the other. When revived she spread the alarm, and an intelligent pursuit followed, as the survivor knew the murderer and described him accurately. To-night a telegram was received at Atlanta saying that Hudson is in jail at Albany, Ga., and asking for military aid to prevent the crowd from lynching him. Mr. Lee was found dead in the house, with his head split open.

HENRY SMITH was hanged at Corinth, Miss., on the 18th, for the murder of a comrade named Burt, in April, 1880. THIRTY-TWO deaths had occurred up to the 20th as the result of the recent tornado at New Ulm, Minn., and vicinity. Great destitution exists, which is being relieved by contributions from nearly all parts of the country.

T. L. BRAYTON, United States Deputy Collector of Internal Revenue, was murdered by illicit distillers in Pickens County, S. C., on the 20th.

JOHN EBERLY committed suicide on his wife's grave at Marion, O.

An express train on the Delaware & Hudson Railway struck a rock, near Dresden, N. Y., on the 21st, three cars leaving the track. Charles Carswell, engineer, was killed, and the fireman and two passengers were injured.

A rock slide in the Washington quarry, near Slatington, Pa., resulted in the death of Wm. Coffin and Charles Erdman.

Mrs. Merks and Miss Blitz were killed by runaway horses in Jersey City, N.J.

A yacht containing six young men belonging to South Boston, Mass., capsized and all were drowned.

The open cut of the Caledonia mine, at Terraville, D. T., caved in on the 20th, burying seven miners. Wm. Gill, Daniel Cameron and Andrew Latson were taken out alive. John Costello, James Roach, Pat Hawkins and L. H. Hamilton are supposed to be killed.

At Fall River, Mass., Andrew Johnson, John Howard and Joseph Yates, all boys, were drowned while bathing. An 11-year-old son of M. H. Cushing met the same fate at Middleboro.

The Perryville (Ark.) vendetta has broken out afresh, the latest victim being Mr. Mathews, editor of the Perryville Times, who was shot while standing in front of his office on the evening of the 21st, sixteen buckshot entering his side.
JOHN WILSON, while in a state of somnambulism, walked out of the second-story window of a hotel in Dallas, Texas, and sustained fatal injuries.

The monument to the Confederate dead at Culpeper, Va., was unveiled on the 21st in the presence of several thousand people, with appropriate ceremonies.

The Secretary of the Treasury has awarded the gold life-saving medal to the famous Ida Lewis, now Mrs. Ida Lewis Wilson, in recognition of her services in rescuing a number of persons from drowning since the passage of the act authorizing such awards.

There was a general jail delivery at Ozark, Ark., the other night, by which four prisoners, on trial for murder, with every prospect of conviction, were set free. A jail guard is said to have opened the door.

THOMAS DEVITT and Legrande Ensign have been arrested in Philadelphia for complicity in Star-route postal frauds. Other arrests are to follow.

The Socialistic Congress, which was prohibited at Zurich, assembled at London on the 19th. Louise Michel, the amnestied French Communist, Prince Krapetkine, the Russian Nihilist, and other prominent leaders were in attendance. The Navajos are so greatly dissatisfied with their Agent, Galen Eastman, that they have risen in open mutiny, and all the Agency employees have fled from Fort Defiance to Fort Wingate for protection. The Indians want Col. Edward Hatch reinstated as Agent.

The National Educational Association met at Atlanta, Ga., on the 19th. The address of welcome was delivered by Governor Colquitt and the inaugural address by the President of the Association, J. H. Smart, of Indiana. Two hundred delegates were present, representing thirty States.

The town of Wallace, Wis., sixteen miles north of Menominee, has been destroyed by fire. It comprised a saw-mill and twenty-five dwelling-houses.

ORIGIN OF THE DIFFICULTY.
One account furnished us states that the riot originated in the following manner: On Saturday the 13th instant a young man named Coulbourn was passing Dana's marine railway when he asked a colored man in Dana's employ, at work in a scow, to do him a favor, but Dana objected and Coulbourn boarded the scow to thrash the man for refusing. The colored man got the advantage and several of Coulbourn's friends started to his aid in a skiff; on seeing which the colored man, though unable to swim, jumped overboard. A peaceable and industrious colored man started to the assistance of the drowning man who was however rescued when nearly drowned by the party in the skiff. A few words passed between the crowd and Tucker, but the latter went away to his work. On last Friday night a party of white men who had been drinking freely was standing in front of Blizzard's bebaving in a disorderly manner, when Tucker passed by. According to reliable eye witnesses, John Holland said to him, Tucker, you d—s—of a b—you'll not stay here long. Tucker foolishly stopped to argue the point when he received heavy blows on the head with some hard weapon. He put his hand to his head and ran saying "Oh my God! I'm nearly murdered.—Rumor says George Holland ran after him to the corner of the alley and stood behind a new house and then with his right hand, head and neck in the alley fired several shots down the alley. While so shooting the shots were returned by some unknown and invisible person from an upstairs window, probably, when Holland was seriously wounded. The alley is inhabited by a number of colored folks. The above account appears to be the origin of the greatly to-be-regretted affair which led to another out-break on Saturday night. At last accounts the town was very much excited, but precaution was taken to prevent further disturbance.—Somerset Herald.

PAUPERS.

The Indianapolis Poor-Farm Investigation Still in Progress—Evidence for the Defense.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

INDIANAPOLIS, Ind., July 6.—The Poor-Farm investigation still drags its slow length along, notwithstanding the excessive heat of the past few days. The defense scored some good points to-day, introducing a number of prominent business-men who have supplied the institution with meat, bread, and provisions, who uniformly testified that the articles furnished, while not always the highest in price, were sound and good. A number of witnesses were introduced to prove the good character of Superintendent Wright for peace, quiet, and humanity, and to show that the asylum was clean and well kept, and the inmates properly cared for. Ilbram W. Waller, Trustee of Wayne Township, while testifying to the peaceable character of Wright, admitted on cross-examination that he thought Wright had been more severe in his discipline than his predecessor. The defense say they have a large number of witnesses yet to call, and that the evidence will take until the end of the week.

A TRAGEDY IN HARTWELL, GA.
Henry Hill, a Negro Prisoner, Kills T. V. Skelton, the Jailor, and Escapes Jail.
From the Hartwell (Ga.) Sun.
On the night of the 23d ultimo, just after sunset, Mr. Thomas V. Skelton, the jailor of Hart County, went into the jail to feed and water Henry Hill, alias Henry Turner, colored, who was the only occupant, and who has been confined therein for some months under a charge of burglary, preferred against him by the Grand Jury at the last term of Hart Superior Court. Mr. Skelton had left his store just about sunset, remarking to Mr. J. L. Snipes, his copartner, that he was going to attend to the prisoner and go home early, as his wife was in great distress, having just heard of the death of her brother, Mr. N. K. Sullivan, of Anderson, S. C. Mr. Snipes thought nothing strange of his not returning to the store, and Mrs. Skelton, supposing that her husband was at the store, suffered no great uneasiness. About eight o'clock at night Mr. Snipes needed a key which Mr. Skelton had, and sent a note up to Mr. Skelton's requesting him to send the key, when it was ascertained that Mr. Skelton was not at home. This caused considerable uneasiness, and after search had been made at the various stores in town, Mr. Dobbins, the clerk of Mr. Skelton, and others, went to the jail and found the outer door open. They entered and ascended the stairway to the inner door, which opens into the hall fronting the cells. They found that open, and just inside the hall door lay the dead body of poor Tom Skelton, his head horribly and cruelly mangled, and Henry gone. Next morning Mr. Allan McGee, the Coroner, summoned an inquest, and after hearing the evidence the jury rendered a verdict, that Thomas V. Skelton was murdered by Henry Hill, alias Henry Turner, and recommended that the Governor offer a reward of five hundred dollars for his apprehension. The manner in which the prisoner succeeded in accomplishing his hellish scheme seems to have been as follows: During last fall he attempted to make his escape by burning the jail, but was detected before he succeeded. After this he was put in another cell and chained until a short time ago, he got to limping and complaining so much that Mr. Skelton, through his kindness of heart, removed the chains from his limbs, but still kept him confined in the cell. The chain was left in the cell fastened to the floor, which Henry succeeded in breaking off, the portion of the chain link where it was broken being left as sharp as a dull pocket knife. There is a small wicket or trap-door in the cell large enough for an ordinary man to squeeze through, which is used for passing food, water, &c., into the cell without opening the door (both the wicket and cell door are made of large iron bars). The wicket is fastened by a strong lock to a large bolt staple driven ten inches into the huge side timbers of the door. With the piece of chain he went to work, and by degrees tediously cut out the wood across the inner framing of the cell door so that he could drive out the large staple, lock and all, that confined the wicket. As his work progressed he would fill the trench with cotton and carefully smooth it over with the lime that had been put in his cell for disinfecting purposes so there would be no danger of being detected, hiding his work from the outside of the cell. Having cut around the staple sufficiently, he pushed it out and that enabled him to crawl out of the cell into the hallway in front of the cells through the trap-door. He was then in position to plan fully his purpose. He armed himself with pieces of plank torn from his bunk, and from the appearance of the surroundings it is likely that he took his position in the corner of the hall between the door entering the hall and the door of the cell, the one he occupied being the first one on the right as you enter, and quietly awaited the approach of his victim. Mr. Skelton unlocked the hall door, and, with a bucket of water in his hand, entered to approach the cell door, and doubtless as he took his first step into the hall received the merciless blow of the concealed assassin, who, throttling him with his left hand, dealt the blow with his right. There were marks on the murdered man's neck as if he had been choked, and ten distinct gashes on his head, which was crushed most fearfully, and indications showed that while Mr. Skelton was partially stunned by the first blow, he had not met his death without a desperate struggle, but he could not cope with the infuriated negro, who has immense strength. And there the poor man lay in death with his face resting in a large pool of clotted gore. TUGALOO HOME, April 25, 1881.

Messrs. Editors: Having some business at Hartwell I made it convenient to attend to it on Friday, the day of the "hanging," and propose a "pen picture" of what I saw and heard on that day, if you deem them worthy of publication. I set out early on Friday morning, the prospect for enjoyment being gloomy in consequence of lowering clouds and fog; but as the day advanced the sun broke out and the day was lovely and summer-like. We had not traveled far before we were convinced that we were not the only one going to Hartwell on that occasion. The road was literally crowded with all kinds of vehicles, horseback and pedestrians, without regard to sex, color or previous condition, all hurrying pell-mell, "going to the hanging." When we reached Hartwell the public square presented more the appearance of a division review than a collection of civilians. The crowd increased from every road leading to Hartwell until near 12 o'clock, at which time the excursion train arrived, which ended the influx of the already immense throng of people. Between 12 and 1 o'clock the condemned culprit was brought from his cell by the Sheriff, amid the screams and wailings of the prisoner's children and friends and placed in a wagon containing his coffin and driven to the gallows, under the escort of a strong guard. Amid the pathetic screams some one chimed in, who had embibed pretty freely of tangle-leg, "Dem golden slippers I'm 'bout to wear!" The prisoner ascended the steps of the gallows in charge of the Sheriff and his deputy, accompanied by Revs. Thornton and Farris and Dr. Eberhart. The prisoner was almost speechless with emotion when given the opportunity to speak. The prisoner, after several efforts to speak, recovered his self possession and beckoned to the crowd and there pervaded a breathless silence throughout the vast concourse of people. I was not prepared to take notes, but write from memory, and cannot remember all that was said; but he made some well-timed remarks, notwithstanding they came from the uncultured lips of a sable African. He addressed his children first and told them never to carry a deck of cards with a little flask of whiskey in the side pocket, for they have placed this rope around my neck. He was a notorious gambler and was said to be an expert. He played and lost until he was forced to pilfer and was lodged in prison and to make his escape killed his "best friend." He acknowledged to the deed and seemed to be truly penitent and expressed himself prepared to meet his God in peace. There was nothing in his demeanor or language that was sarcastic or antagonistic, and although the murder was premeditated, cold-blooded and wilful, yet to witness the last imposing scenes of the felon, with the noose around his neck, imploring forgiveness, no doubt had a tendency to appease, if it were possible, the animosity aroused in the hearts of the people by the heinous and foul deed! Many a stout heart was melted to tears as the Rev. Mr. Thornton read and sang,

"Alas! and did my Saviour bleed," &c., followed in prayer by Rev. Mr. Farris. When the hymn was read the prisoner requested everybody to sing. After taking an affectionate leave of his family he bid the white people farewell, his hands were tied behind him, his legs tied together, the cap that shut out the light forever was pulled over his face, a chord was fastened to the trigger and pulled from under the platform with these words from the executioner, "Farewell Henry." and Henry Hill alias Henry Turner at half-past 1 o'clock suffered the extreme penalty of the law. This is but another sad commentary on the use of strong drink. Although it was not the exciting cause, but it was no doubt the predisposing or indirect cause that led to the foul deed. After hanging thirty minutes the dead body was taken down and placed in the coffin and delivered to his friends. The crowd was large and orderly. An ex-Sheriff who had adjusted the noose on similar occasions supposed there were 8,000 persons present, but I think there were not more than 5,000.

He had a large sum of silver wrapped in a handkerchief, and was counting it, when a negro suddenly stopped out from the adjacent woods and asked for change for a $100 Confederate bill. Waters declined, and was moving away, when the negro sprang upon him. A desperate struggle ensued. The negro struck him on the head, falling him on the ground, and Waters, fearing he would be murdered, feigned death and allowed the rullan to rile his pockets. After the thief had fled with his booty, Waters crawled half a mile to the nearest house and related the circumstances, minutely describing his assailant. On his person was found a $100 Confederate bill, several $10 bills, and a large amount of silver, though the bulk of the sum stolen from Waters was missing. The night succeeding his incarceration a party of ten masked men surrounded the jail and forced the jailer to lead them to Pettis' cell. They took the prisoner to a woods some distance from town, and told him that his life would be spared only on condition he led them to the spot where he had hid the balance of the money taken from Waters. At first Pettis denied all knowledge of the matter; a rope was placed around his neck and thrown over a limb, and he was drawn up and let down three times in rapid succession. The miserable wretch then made a full confession, the main facts of which have already been related, and led the mob to a dense thicket in the heart of the woods where he had secreted the proceeds of the robbery. PLUCKY PETE.
A Mob Attempts to Lynch a Murderer in the Hands of Sheriff J. P. Gabriel-A Determined and Successful Resistance.
On Sunday last a ruffian, who gave his name as J. H. Floyd, shot and instantly killed American Charley, a well known citizen of Florence. The deed was committed in cold blood, and under such circumstances as to rouse the spirit of summary vengeance in the people of that place, and they immediately organized with the intention of lynching the murderer.

Sheriff J. P. Gabriel, who had the prisoner in charge, anticipated the movement, and in broad daylight yesterday took Floyd to Casa Grande, en route to Tucson, for safe keeping. He was followed by a party of determined men from Florence, who took him by surprise and at a disadvantage, and with leveled guns at his breast demanded of him the prisoner. Without flinching or exhibiting any fear whatever, the brave officer defied the crowd and refused to comply with their demands, and with sheer superiority of courage kept eight or ten men from accomplishing their purpose. After a time he secured other assistance, and the crowd withdrew for consultation. All night and until the train from the west reached Casa Grande, Sheriff Gabriel maintained his vigilance, and at last succeeded in convincing the crowd of the folly and uselessness of their efforts, just as the train rolled up to the depot. The prisoner was quickly transferred on board and reached this city in safety this morning and was consigned to a dungeon in the county jail.

While there would doubtless have been a merited justice in the swift retribution intended by the indignant citizens, yet when an officer of the law has a plain duty to perform he should be aided in its discharge by all good citizens, however repugnant to their feelings such assistance may be, for when wholesome laws are held in contempt the life and property of every citizen is thereby more or less jeopardized, and a license for other lawlessness tacitly recognized.

Only Manslaughter!
The trial of Floyd, the black-livered brute who, on the 15th day of last May, shot down without excuse or provocation a helpless and harmless old man, was concluded Thursday evening and the jury, after remaining out about twenty minutes, brought in a verdict of "manslaughter!" This result was both a surprise and a disappointment to those conversant with the facts of the case. Before the commencement of the trial there was not even the remotest suspicion here that this hell-deserving dastard would escape expiation of his crime on the gallows. If there ever was a cold-blooded, deliberate murder the killing of Charles Bernard by this man Floyd was one, and there was ample proof of the fact, but unfortunately it was not introduced at the trial. The defense claimed that Bernard invited Floyd to his room and asked him for two dollars and upon being refused struck the defendant over the head with a club and was advancing to strike again when the latter fired in self-defense. This was the statement of Floyd, unsupported by a single witness, and the only evidence offered in his defense, excepting the statement of the officers to the effect that they noticed a bruise on the prisoner's head after he was placed in jail. It could have been proven that this bruise was on his head before he went over to Bernard's room; it could have been pr
boisterous, profane and obscene talk; it could have been proven that he had been expressing a desire, all day, to kill some one and that during the afternoon he plunged his knife into a counter and broke the blade in two, remarking that he would like to stick it into some one's head and break it off that way and that he didn't care a d——n who it was either. But the witnesses who could have testified to these facts were not called into court and this vile and vicious "varmint" in human form, instead of having his neck jerked out of joint as he deserves, goes to Yuma for five years. Great God what a comment on Arizona justice to go abroad!

A TRAVESTY OF JUSTICE.
In yesterday's issue of the CITIZEN, we alluded to some defects in the administration of the laws of the country, which defeat rather than subserve the ends of justice, speaking especially of the jury system as it is now abused. In the same issue we published a dispatch from Florence announcing the conviction of J. H. Floyd, who shot Charles Bernard—better known throughout the Territory as "American Charley"—on the 15th of last May, of manslaughter, and his sentence to five years in the penitentiary. The escape of this man Floyd from the merited punishment for his crime is an outrage on humanity and a travesty of justice.

The circumstances of the crime are briefly as follows: The victim of the murder was quietly seated in the door of his room, when Floyd, crazed with liquor, passed along the street. When opposite where Bernard was sitting, he turned, drew his revolver and shot him dead.

We have no hesitation in pronouncing the verdict and the sentence in this case a mockery of justice. It is certainly a poor guarantee for the safety of human life in this Territory. If crimes of that character can be committed in this country with such impunity then no man's life is safe. The fact that the victim was old and poor, and had outlived his usefulness, if he ever had any, makes no difference with the merits of the case. In fact we do not believe that the murderer had any animosity then no man's li
Bernard the life of every man in that community was assailed and endangered, and on the grounds of public policy a different punishment should have been meted out.

An attempt was made by the outraged people of Florence to lynch the murderer, and in view of the results of the trial it is almost a matter of regret that the intention was not carried out.

There is something radically defective about laws or their administration when such a disparity between the crime and its punishment exists. If the verdict and sentence was all that the law made possible, then the law should be changed. If, on the other hand, it is the administration of justice that is at fault it is high time that it was changed.

Human life is or should be sacred, and it needs stronger guarantees than the verdict and sentence in this case give it.

TWO RASCALS RETURNED,
And They Can Now Get Ready for a Double Hanging.
Little Rock Special to Cincinnati Times Star.

Wm. Casey and Jas. P. Holland have again been jailed at Ozark, whence they escaped four months since. They were captured in Tennessee. Casey has been twice sentenced to hang and Holland once. Both will likely be executed on the same day. In 1879 Holland conspired with Wm. Casey and Chas. G. Helphrey to rob and murder a young and eccentric planter named Burgess James, who was supposed to carry a large amount of money on his person. James was waylaid and brutally shot by Helphrey in Yell county, on the bank of the Arkansas river.

The assassin secured a belt containing some $300, and ran away with the bulk of the money, Casey and Holland getting only $20. James lived long enough to make a deposition that led to the arrest of the trio. Helphrey then gave the plot away. Casey was tried, found guilty, and twice sentenced to be hanged, his doom being averted in the first instance by a new trial, and in the second by an appeal to the Supreme Court.

Holland was placed on trial at the spring term of the Franklin County Circuit Court, held in Ozark. Pending the verdict of the jury he, together with Casey and Helphrey, succeeded in escaping from jail through the treachery of a guard. The fugitives took refuge in the mountains in the vicinity of Ozark, and, though hotly pursued, eluded capture, and when the excitement had abated succeeded in getting out of the State.

GRAYSON, KY., March 29.—Bands of men styling themselves Regulators have inaugurated a reign of terror in portions of this and the adjoining County of Greenup by their unlawful depredations against the public. At Hunnewell Furnace, four miles below here, in Greenup County, on the Eastern Kentucky Railroad, a party of irresponsible ruffians attempted to control the business action of the Furnace Company. Failing in this, they restored to foul means, and the Company has been obliged to arm its employees to protect its property.

About the first of the present month Mr. Sebastian Gifort, Superintendent of the Hunnewell Furnace dispatched his son and clerk, Joseph Gifort, to Virginia to engage a force of ore-diggers. The young man returned with about forty negroes, who were at once put to work on the ore-banks. The employment of these black men incensed the so-called Regulators, and they sent notices to Mr. Gifort and his son to leave the country or suffer the penalty, death. No attention was paid to these anonymous proclamations.

On the night of the 20th inst., about twelve or fifteen of the Regulators met a party of the black-ore diggers in Browntown, near the Furnace. A brisk fight ensued and several shots were fired. One of the negroes received a face wound and a Regulator named Jones received a bullet through his groin. The blacks retreated to the Furnace and claimed protection, whereupon Superintendent Gifort armed about two hundred employees of the Furnace and prepared to give the Regulators battle. Since that time the Furnace property has been watched night and day by armed men. The Regulators threaten death and the destruction of the property by fire. Eight of the band have been arrested and are in jail at Catlettsburg.

One night last week a party of the Regulators went to the house of a man named Bellamy, on the Smoky Fork of the Buffalo Fork of Tygart, in this county, and calling out old man Ballamy and his three sons, administered to each thirty-nine lashes with hickory withes, for alleged immorality. They also whipped two women living in the neighborhood for the same offense. The Regulators were masked and well armed. John Snider, a son-in-law of Bellamy's was threatened with hanging, but he escaped, and is now lying out, afraid to return to his wife and family.

A Battle in the Streets of El Paso.

SANTA FÉ, N. M., April 18. —Last Wednesday afternoon a party of Americans and two Mexicans became engaged in a quarrel at El Paso and the two Mexicans were killed. The affair created great excitement on both sides of the river. The following day armed Mexicans crossed the river to take possession of the bodies of their friends. The Americans showed great indignation at the conduct of the Mexicans; and in a short time organized a party to attack the Mexicans. Meantime the town of Franklin (The American El Paso) was thrown into a state of the wildest excitement, resulting in a conflict between the two parties. The row became general, and bullets flew thick. During the melee John Hall, mistaking one Kremkaw for a Mexican, shot and instantly killed him, and was himself shot by an American. The Town Marshal, having unsuccessfully endeavored to quell the disturbance, took part himself and fatally wounded one Campbell and a Mexican. A number of others were slightly wounded. Since Thursday the towns of El Paso and Franklin have been quiet, and there probably will be no further disturbance.

The serious aspect of affairs, and the certainty that a continuance of riotous demonstrations could have but one result, induced Lieutenant Colonel Woodhouse, Major Deveaux and Adjutant Toomer, of the colored battalion, three well known representative colored men, at the suggestion of some citizens, to go among the strikers and endeavor to check the spirit of insubordination and disorder which was so manifest. They made very conservative speeches, and advised the men, for their own sakes, to refrain from any acts of violence, and to take the peaceable method of petition for the adjustment of their troubles. The men listened with attention, and showed a disposition to act on the advice given, and it was decided to ask a committee of citizens to confer with Col. Wadley and ascertain what arrangements could be made. Captain John Flannery, Colonel J. H. Estill and L. H. DeMontmollin, Esq., consented to act as mediators, and at once proceeded to the railroad wharf, where they had an interview with Col. Wadley, who, after hearing the proposition of the strikers, replied that he was perfectly willing for the men to return to work at once, and then after this affair had quieted down, if they had any petition to make he would give it consideration, but under no circumstances would he make any promises as to his future course. Meanwhile a communication had been addressed by the Chairman of the strikers to a number of prominent Bay street merchants, requesting them to intercede with the employers with the view of effecting a satisfactory adjustment of the difficulty, which they agreed to do.

In the afternoon at 5 o'clock, an immense mass meeting of colored men was held at the foot of Bryan street, which was addressed by the colored officers above mentioned in the same style as in the morning, and afterwards by Mr. DeMontmollin, who stated the result of the interview with Colonel Wadley. The men seemed inclined favorably to take the course suggested—return to work at the old rates, and petition for an increase in a proper manner, but, after some discussion, it was decided to wait until 12 o'clock this morning to ascertain what had been accomplished by the other committee. The indications are that the negotiations will be successful, and that the troubles will be ended to-day, as the laborers will perceive that the only possible way to succeed in securing an advance in their wages is to adopt the course referred to, return quietly to their work and then make a respectful presentation of their claims for an increase. The more sensible among them are awakening to this fact, and as stated, there is good reason to anticipate an adjustment to-day.

On Monday morning, the 19th inst., the negro laborers loading the steamship Gate City at Savannah, struck for $2 per day, and on being refused quit work. Those on the steamship Dessong continued until 1 p. m. When they came back nearly all of them were drunk and wouldn't work or allow others to do so. The officer, being mounted, arrived before the others, and was at once attacked by a crowd of negroes. In the melee one of the mob shot the officer, inflicting, what is supposed to be, a mortal wound. A reinforcement of police arrived and dispersed the rioters, though they gathered several times afterwards and made demonstrations to interfere with the men at work. The ships were loaded under the protection of the police. The employers manifested a determination to resist the demands of the strikers to the bitter end, and employed new hands. The trouble continued from time to time during the whole of last week, the strikers making several demonstrations. On Thursday a skirmish took place between the police and the rioters, resulting in several casualties, and the temporary dispersal of the rioters. Later an attempt was made to harmonize matters by a committee of old citizens, acting at the request of the strikers, but it failed, as the strikers would not agree to the terms adopted by said committee.

Negroes Taken from Jail and Hung while their Trial was in Progress.
SPRINGFIELD, Tenn., Feb. 19.—On the night of Sept. 8 last a farmer named Laprade was murdered. He lived alone, in the neighborhood of Sadlersville, Robinson County, and was supposed to have a hoard of money. A party of negroes went to his house, and tortured him horribly to make him confess where the money was concealed, which he protested he did not have. He was burned with torches, cut with knives, and strung up by the neck repeatedly. Finally his skull was crushed in with an axe, and the body thrown into a sink hole.

The murder caused intense excitement. An old negro named James Higgins was suspected of having been concerned in it. He was arrested and made statements inculpating other negroes. A party of lynchers took him out and roasted his feet until he made a full confession. Higgins had to have one of his feet amputated, and subsequently died in jail.

On the night of Sept. 15 two others of those who had been arrested on charge of the murder, Bell and Jamieson, were taken from jail and lynched, and at the same time a white man named Ramsey was shot to death in his cell. He was awaiting trial for shooting a Miss Holt because she had rejected him for another suitor.

After these events the excitement quieted down, and it looked as if the regular course of justice would not be interfered with in the case of the remaining prisoners. The lynching feeling was, however, revived by the report that the accused were to be granted a change of venue. On the night of the 14th inst. a party of mounted men rode into town and made for the jail. They had broken in the door when Judge Stork and Attorney-General Bell arrived and addressed the mob, urging them to refrain from lawless behavior, and pledging them that the prisoners should be punished to the full extent of the law if found guilty. The Attorney-General assured them that he would conduct the prosecution with the greatest possible energy.

The lynchers seemed to be satisfied by these assurances and dispersed; but it was thought best to have a company of State troops in attendance when the trial began. Two of the accused, Bill Murphy and Anthony Duffy, testified for the State. They were released last Thursday, and immediately returned to their former haunts. This stirred up the lynch-law feeling again.

The militia company gave a parade in the Court House yard before dark last night. After dark a furious thunder storm set in, and fear of lynching the prisoners vanished. A night session of the court was held to finish the trial, and Judge Stark gave his charge to the jury, after which the Sheriff proceeded with the prisoners—James Higgins, Lock Mallory, Lon. Thiveat, Robert Thiveat, and James Elder—to the jail. A mob of about two hundred pressed upon the Sheriff, took the prisoners, cleared the Court House and grounds, stationed a strong picket guard around them, and hung them from the second-story windows of the Court House.

The onset of the mob was so sudden and boisterous, accompanied by firing of pistols and guns into the air, as to terrify the spectators in the court room, who jumped from the windows and hastened from the scene. The lynchers numbered 200 well-armed men, who came in from three directions on horseback, and dispersed in the same manner. And Snatch the Five Laprade Murderers from Custody,
Before the Judge Had Hardly Completed His Charge.
They are Hanged from a Second- Story Window.
The Two Who Turned State's Evidence Reported Lynched Also.
Special Dispatch to the Chronicle.
NASHVILLE, Feb. 19.

The lynching of the five Laprade murders, colored, at Springfield, has created a profound sensation here. The judge had just concluded his charge to the jury last night when the mob rushed into the court room and seized the prisoners, who were about to be conveyed to jail by the sheriff, and hurried them to the veranda of the second story, where nooses had quietly been provided. They placed the nooses around the necks of the prisoners and threw them over.

When the mob entered the court room, the officers attempted to defend the prisoners, but were intimidated by pistols placed at their head. The spectators were thrown into consternation, retiring hastily through the windows of the court room. The mob would not permit any one to come near the bodies of the murderers until they were sure they were dead. At least two hundred shots were fired in order to intimidate the people, but none at the prisoners. The murderers were left hanging until 8 a.m. to day, when they were cut down. The spectacle presented before the bodies were cut down was sickening.

It is reported that Duffy, one of the negroes who turned State's evidence, was also hanged last night, he having gone back into the neighborhood where the murder was committed with Murphy, who had been released on the evening previous.

The two Joes, murderers of Baker, were brought here to-night from Winchester, Penn, having waived examination. They were guarded by the military, who were followed to the depot at Winchester by an indignant, threatening assemblage of three hundred people.

The prisoners were then taken out of the hands of the guards, carried to the door steps, over which is a balcony, from which swung five ropes with a hangman's noose in the end of each.

Jim Elder, one of the prisoners, had to be thrown down before he was mastered. The ropes were adjusted, all lights extinguished, and the command, "Heave away, boys," rent the air. At this order strong arms in the balcony suspended the bodies of the men between heaven and earth, in which position they remained until 9 o'clock this morning.

The commander asked, after a period of half an hour, perhaps: "Are you satisfied?" "Yes!" was responded by a hundred voices. A volley of pistol shots was fired and three cheers of exultation were given by order of the command, when they were ordered to disperse to their homes, which they did, going three different directions.

THE CORONER'S INQUEST.

The Coroner's inquest was held this morning, with a verdict of "came to their death by the hands of unknown persons." All men acquainted with the evidence In this case, regardless of color, say they were guilty. Your reporter heard some of our best colored men remark, "It was too easy a death, was too quick; they should have suffered the same tortures that they inflicted upon Laprade, before they were hanged."

THE HERMIT VICTIM.

About fourteen miles from this place, in a western direction, lazily sleeps the quiet little village bearing the name of Sadersville. A half mile, or perhaps a furlong or so more, on a little farm, lived Leonidas S. Laprade. He resided all alone. So eccentric was his character that he would not allow a hog, dog, chicken or cat upon his place—no living animal except his two horses. It is said that even the sight of a living thing on his farm would dreadfully annoy him, and his happy moments were those when shut out in his little house from all the world. He did his own cooking, and, in fact, attended to everything connected with household duties. Nobody disliked him particularly, and so far as is known he had no enemies. He had resided on his little farm a number of years, and, as might be supposed from his mode of living, attended strictly and closely to his own business.

THE INCENTIVE TO THE MURDER.

Last July a rumor was circulated that old man Laprade and his brother had fallen heirs, by the death of a relative in France, to $9,000, and that they had received the money, which was equally divided between the two, and that the hermit had his part of the money secreted in his house. The rumor as are many rumors, was a lie, and just how it came to be circulated no one yet knows, but it was a fatal rumor for Laprade.

THE MURDERERS.

In the Sadlersville district there was a nest of bad niggers, who lived by stealing from their neighbors and were frequently engaged in drunken and disgraceful broils. These bad negroes heard the rumor about Laprade's money and formed a plot to murder and rob him. Now comes the horrible part of my story.

THE MURDER.

On the night of August 30, 1880, an hour past midnight, Laprade was awakened by a knock on his door. "Who's there?" he cried in a startled voice, jumping out of bed and coming to the door. "It's me, Lon, let me in," answered a voice like his brother. Supposing it was his brother, Laprade opened the door, when four negroes rushed in and seized him. There were five in the yard surrounding the house and one at the front gate posted as outside sentinel—ten savages in all against one weak, old man. They demanded his money or his life. He told them that he had no money, and for God's sake to spare his life. They laughed mockingly at his denial and slapped him in the face (Remember, reader, that I write from the evidence of one of the fiends, who turned State's witness and from the confessions of two others who were hung.) A rope was thrown around his neck and he was dragged out of the house into the yard. Here he was brutally beaten and kicked and pulled through the yard across a field to a rail fence. In the meantime the poor victim of the devil's agents was moaning with pain and begging piteously for mercy. He wore long hair, and his whiskers hung down half a foot before. The human monsters stripped from the rail fencing pieces of splinters, and igniting them, held the fire brands to his face, singing off his hair and beard and badly burning his face and eyes. "Oh, for the love of God, kill me, boys, and put me out of my pain," was the agonizing cry of the poor, tortured man. Not satisfied with the commission of this most atrocious and horrible cruelty, they next cut a piece of flesh out of his left thigh and another piece out of the calf of the right leg. It would seem that their monstrous work would have stopped here, but not so, for they next cut off the poor dying man's ears. They then dragged him a few hundred yards further, and, building a fire, held his hands over the flames until they were shockingly burned, the poor victim in the meantime grooming and withering in physical agony. Could devilish ingenuity born in hell invent more horrible tortures! It seems not; and yet it did—for one of the fiends beat a hole in his head with a rock, and inserting the blade of a large barlow knife, wrenched it around in the hole. Their next horrible act was to split with a knife the skin on his forehead from ear to ear and then press it back to the roots of his hair, leaving the scalp bare. His body was then dragged to a sink hole and tumbled in. Two of them fearing that he was not yet dead procured a rail and pounded his head and breast into a jelly. Then agreeing upon a plan for proving an alibi, if they were suspected of the bloody crime, the murderers separated.

THE BODY DISCOVERED.

The second day afterward Laprade was missed from his house and search instituted. On the third day his mutilated body was found in the old sink hole, half a mile away from his home, and a thrill of horror shot through the frame of every citizen of Robertson county. It was too horrible to be true, and many citizens would not believe it until they had seen with their own eyes the mutilated form of the murdered victim. Then horror gave way to a fixed and determined purpose that the bloody, merciless fiends should be hunted down and that there should be no let up in the search until the last one connected with the crime should suffer death. The avengers were on the track of the murderers, and they constituted the most determined men in the county.

THE TRAIL STRUCK.

In the meantime suspicion fastened upon a band of bad negroes near the scene of the murder, and particularly upon one Jack Bell. He was known to be one of the worst

negroes in the State, capable of committing any crime. He was arrested and brought to the jail in this place. A day or so after his arrest Jim Higgins, a negro preacher, told another negro that Jack Bell and Archie Jamison would tell lies on him if they had a chance. This led to the arrest of Archie Jamison, and he was thrown into the county jail with his pal, Bell. During this time citizen detectives had not been idle, and they had obtained strong circumstantial evidence against both Bell and Jamison.

THREE VICTIMS SECURED.

One night, the first week in September, I think, a body of men marched into the town of Springfield, and, going to the jail, demanded Bell and Jamison. The keys of the jail being refused them, they repaired to a neighboring blacksmith shop, and, procuring heavy sle

A jury was empaneled Tuesday and the trial at once proceeded. Two of the murderers turned State's evidence and gave graphic details of the horrible murder of Laprade. Following is the evidence of Duffy:

I lived with Bob Daniel, in Robertson county; left Mr. Daniel on Saturday, in August; went to Bell's Chapel, Sunday, and hired myself to Mr. Jim Young; know defendants at the bar.

The witness then pointed the prisoners out and identified them, and told where each had lived previous to the killing of Laprade. He continued:

Bell's Chapel was one mile back of Jim Higgins' house; saw there the prisoner Jim Higgins and the other prisoners, ten in all—Bob. Threat, Arch Jamison, Lun Small, Lock Mallory, Jim Elder, Jack Bell,——Mallory (and two others whose names the reporter could not get), we met at the forks of the road to make arrangements to kill Laprade; had a meeting previous to this for the same purpose; Jack Bell was the first to mention the matter to me; he told me that Jim Higgins and Arch Jamison had formed a conspiracy to kill Mr. Laprade; they believed he had money; there were present Jack Bell, Arch Jamison, Jim Higgins and myself at Higgins' house, and we agreed to help each other out of the difficulty in case any of us should be arrested; I knew Laprade; he was thrown into a sink hole on the Monday night after he was killed by (here witness repeated the names before mentioned); Jack Bell told me Laprade had money and we must kill him and get it; we held a meeting at Higgins' house and agreed to meet at the cross roads and proceed to Laprade's and kill him; Arch Jamison selected the sink hole as the place to hide the body: we met about 1 o'clock in the night; Jack Bell said, "we will kill him and put him in the sink-hole." went to the house; Bill Murphy stopped at the gate; Lun Small and myself stood in the yard; Jim Higgins, Bell and Jamison went into the house; I heard Laprade begging for his life and saying he had no money; they brought him out of the house with a rope around his neck, took him across the field and lifted him over the fence; Jack Bell cut off his private parts saying, "I have cut many a d—d hog and I'll cut you;" Jim Higgins cut the skin off his face; Bob Threat cut his leg; Jack Bell hit him in the head with a sharp rock and knocked out his teeth; Jack Bell, after cutting out his privates, cut the skin around the hole in his head; we then dispersed, and I went to Mr. Young's; Jack Bell went with me; when we got to Mr. Young's, Jack asked, "Do you think that man is dead? I will take a rail off the fence and go back and punch him some;" while at the sink hole we were about to drag him farther into the hole, when we heard a noise and Bob Threat and Lun Small ran off.

The other negroe's evidence corroborated all these horrid facts, and more, and the circumstantial evidence was complete, leaving no room for doubt. The trial proceeded regularly until all the evidence was in, the lawyers had spoken and the judge charged the jury. It was just about dusk on Friday evening when the judge finished his charge, and the sheriff was about to start to jail with the prisoners, when about two hundred men rushed into the court-room with presented pistols, ordered the lights out, seized the prisoners and rushed them out.

Attorney-General Bell tried to obtain a posse to stop the mob at the door, but failed, and had to make his exit through a window. The crowd in the court all jumped from the windows.

The negroes were hurried to the east door of the court-house, where ropes were awaiting them, and they were drawn up by willing hands in the verandah above.

They all died without a struggle, except Jim Elder, who had to be thrown down, tied and then raised. Hundreds of shots were fired, but none at the prisoners.

The mob guarded the bodies until they were sure they were dead, and the leader gave the order, "Disperse, my men, to your homes," and they immediately departed, going in three directions.

They came in on horses, but went to the court-house on foot and were not discovered till they met the prisoners at the door.

It is thought that the cause of this trouble to night was the releasing of Bill Murphy and Anthony Duffy, at 12 o'clock last night. When released, they went right back into the vicinity where they committed their terrible crime and were seen there to-day. The people, fearing the prisoners would appeal from the verdict of the jury, and then, it the case was sent back, the State would have no witnesses, and were determined there should be no escape, for beyond a doubt, they were guilty. This is the verdict of every citizen who heard the testimony.

There was no whisky in the crowd, and they were under strict discipline. The only demonstration was a deafening yell and the dis charge of firearms, when the five were launched into eternity. No outsider was allowed to approach the scene until all the negroes were pronounced dead, and then it was announced that the man who cut them down would do so at his peril.
springfield-springfield.A30:
THE REIGN OF LAWLESSNESS.
The legislature passed a resolution unanimously condemning the action of the mob at Springfield in taking prisoners from the custody of the court and putting them to death, and declaring that mobs must be suppressed if it takes the whole power of the state. The resolution calls upon the governor to use all means for the arrest and punishment of the perpetrators of this outrage, and promising the active co-operation of the legislature.

Certainly if human creatures ever deserved lynching it was the demons who murdered Laprade, but our Robertson county friends should bear in mind that mob law is not a remedy for anything. Lawlessness the world over, begets lawlessness. When men trample the law under foot, no matter how just the provocation, they encourage others to do the same. They set an example, which they may rest assured the deprived and violent portion of the community will not be slow to follow. Let the law be a terror to evil doers, and let good citizens everywhere look to the law to ferret out crime and punish criminals. If our criminal laws are defective amend them. If our officials fail in their duty, put better men in their places. Above all things, if we desire a roof to remain over our heads, if we desire our families to go unharmed, if we desire to protect our lives from the assassin, let us uphold the law. Ten men have been hung by a mob in Robertson county in the last two years. The previous lynching did not deter the Laprade fiends from their terrible crime. The last hanging will not have any other effect than to breed contempt for the law in the minds of evil-disposed persons. By all means, let lawiessness of all kinds, whether it be done by the mob in the name of justice, or by the hardened criminal in defiance of justice, be suppressed by the iron hand of the law.
springfield-springfield.A31:
Particulars of the Springfield Lynching.
Five of the seven negroes who were taken from the Nashville jail, back to Springfield, to stand their trial, for the murder of Laprade, were taken from the hands of the law there last Friday evening, the 18th, and lynched. The other two, Murphy and Duffy, who had turned states evidence, and had been released, made their escape, or else they would have shared the same fate. The American's special correspondent, gives the following detailed account of the horrible affair:

SPRINGEIELD, Feb. 19.—The mob has now gone home. There must have been two hundred men. They met the sheriff at the court-room door, with presented pistols, took the prisoners from him and ordered the lights all out. They then carried all five of the negroes to the east door of the court-house, where ropes were awaiting them, and they were drawn up by willing hands in the veranda above.

They all died without a struggle, except Jim Elder, who had to be thrown down, tied and then raised. Hundreds of shots were fired, but none at the prisoners.

The mob guarded the bodies until they were sure they were dead, and the leader gave the order, "disperse my men, to your homes," and they immediately departed, going in three directions.

They came in on horses, but went to the conrt-house, on foot and were not discovered till they met the prisoners at the door.

It is thought that the cause of this trouble to-night, was the releasing of Bill Murphy and Anthony Duffy, at 12 o'clock last night. When released they went right back into the vicinity where they had committed their terrible crime and were seen there to-day. The people, fearing the prisoners would appeal from the verdict of the jury, and then, if the case was sent back, the state would have no witnesses, and determined there should be no escape for, beyond a doubt, they were guilty. This is the verdict of every citizen who heard the testimony.

It is also thought Murphy and Duffy will be caught and lynched to-night. It was not generally known that they were released, but when they were seen to-day, the news spread rapidly, and the people came in to-night and wreaked a terrible vengeance upon the remaining five.

There was no whisky in the crowd, and they were under strict discipline. The only demonstration was a deafening yell and the discharge of fire arms, when the five were launched into eternity. No outsider was allowed to approach the scene until all the negroes were pronounced dead, and then it was announced that the man who cut them down did so at his peril.

When I went to the square the second time, I had no trouble getting to the court-house, and examined the bodies. They are all suspended from the small varanda, close together. Higgins and Elder, in their death struggle, got their ropes twisted and they now hang seemingly from the same rope.

This makes ten men lynched in Springfield within the last two years, two of them Sadler and Pearson, it is believed, were innocent. Ramsay was killed for shooting a young lady who is now alive, but the last seven were guilty and deserved their fate, and I believe a jury would have said so had they bren given a few more hours' time; but an outraged community could wait no longer, and to-night put to death the perpetrators of the most horrible crime that ever blackened the records of our country.
